Chapter 3: The Nature of Anxiety and the Cost of Escaping the Present
Have you ever noticed how anxiety can feel like a shadow, quietly trailing behind you?
It’s not always dramatic or loud—sometimes, it’s just this subtle, nagging sense of unease you can’t quite put your finger on.
Most of us try to outrun that feeling. We stay busy, make endless plans, or distract ourselves with anything we can find. But here’s the thing: the more we avoid it, the more stubborn it gets.
At the heart of anxiety, there’s this deep resistance to being present. Our minds are almost always racing—either worrying about what could go wrong in the future, or replaying regrets from the past. Rarely do we just settle into what’s happening right now. And honestly, this habit feels so normal that we hardly question it. But it does come with a price.
Picture a student, stressed about upcoming exams. Even though the test is days away, they’re lying awake at night, imagining every possible way it could go wrong. The anxiety feels real, and it’s happening now—even though the actual event hasn’t arrived. The mind, trying to prepare, ends up creating a storm of worry that wipes out any chance of rest. In chasing after the future, the present moment slips away.
And it’s not just in crisis moments. Even in everyday life, we tend to postpone our happiness. Maybe you’ve caught yourself thinking, “I’ll relax once I finish this project,” or “I’ll be happy when I finally reach that goal.” But the finish line keeps moving, doesn’t it? There’s always another task, another hurdle, another worry waiting around the corner.
Our culture makes this habit even stronger. With technology, we have endless ways to distract ourselves—scrolling through social media, binge-watching shows, filling up every spare moment with noise. It’s so easy to avoid silence, to keep moving, just so those uncomfortable feelings don’t catch up.
But what’s the cost? The more we neglect the present, the more disconnected we feel from our own lives. Joy turns into something we chase, rather than something we actually experience. Relationships can suffer, creativity dries up, and that sense of meaning—well, it just starts to fade.
There’s this story about a traveler who spends years searching for peace. They visit temples, read every book they can find, and seek out wise teachers. But no matter where they go, that same restlessness tags along. It’s only when they finally stop running, and sit quietly with their discomfort, that something shifts. The peace they were searching for wasn’t out there. It was always within them, hidden beneath all the noise.
Most people don’t realize that anxiety isn’t a flaw—it’s actually a signal. It’s pointing out the gap between how things are, and how we wish they could be. The mind resists what is, and that resistance is where suffering grows. But if we’re willing to face the present moment, even with all its uncertainty, anxiety’s grip starts to loosen.
Now, that doesn’t mean pain or difficulty just disappears. Life will always have its challenges. But there’s a real difference between feeling discomfort, and being completely consumed by it. When we bring our attention back to the present, there’s a sense of grounding. It’s like a reminder that, right now, things are actually manageable.
Imagine a parent, totally worn out after a long day, sitting down with their child as the sun sets. There’s no agenda, no rush. For a few minutes, tomorrow’s worries fade away, and just being together brings this quiet, simple joy. It’s in moments like this that the wisdom of presence really shines through.
The cost of escaping the present is high, but the reward for returning? It’s even greater. Anxiety starts to lose its power when we meet it with attention, instead of avoidance. The present, with all its imperfections, becomes a place of real possibility.
